cards.explanation: The answer is that they defiled it. Asaph, the psalm's writer, tells God the nations "…have defiled Your holy temple…" He says it right to God in the same breath as the rubble. It's the temple, God's own house, and he doesn't water it down, friends.
The word is bury. Asaph says "…there is no one to bury the dead." This is a heavy line, friends, and I think it hurts to read. He doesn't dress it up. He just lays it before God.

The answer is the nations that don't acknowledge Him. Asaph asks God to pour out His wrath "…on the nations that do not acknowledge You…" He adds "…on the kingdoms that refuse to call on Your name…" Both lines point at the same group. His own people aren't in that sentence, friends.

The answer is False. Asaph says the nations "…have devoured Jacob and devastated his homeland." Jacob here is the name for God's people. Their homeland was devastated, friends, so untouched can't be right.
The answer is True. Asaph prays, "Do not hold past sins against us…" Notice he's asking God for mercy, friends, not making excuses. That's a humble way to pray when you're hurting.
The answer is quickly. Asaph says, "let Your compassion come quickly, for we are brought low." He doesn't want to wait around, friends. When you're brought low, you ask for help fast.

The answer is "Where is their God?" Asaph asks why the nations should say that. (Ps 79:10) He doesn't want that question asked, friends. Then he asks God to make known among the nations His vengeance for the bloodshed of His servants.
The answer is captives. Asaph prays, "May the groans of the captives reach You…" These are people held prisoner, and he's asking God to hear them, friends. I think it's a tender line in a hard psalm.

The answer is True. Asaph prays, "by the strength of Your arm preserve those condemned to death." He's asking for God's strength to hold them up. That's a big prayer, friends, and he prays it plainly.
The answer is God Himself. Asaph asks God to pay back "…the reproach they hurled at You, O Lord." The mocking was aimed at God, friends. Sevenfold is what he asks for in return.

The answer is False. Asaph says, "…we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture, will thank You forever…" (Ps 79:13) Forever, friends, not once. Then he adds, "from generation to generation we will declare Your praise."

The answer is the sheep of His pasture. Asaph says, "…we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture…" It's a gentle picture to end on, friends. After all that rubble, he calls them sheep in God's pasture.
